title: The techniques AI uses to create images can help predict floods, researchers say
key_facts: Researchers including Penn State's Chaopeng Shen applied diffusion, the method behind AI image generators, to hourly flash-flood prediction.
Flash floods account for roughly 85% of floods and cause thousands of deaths a year worldwide, per the National Weather Service as cited.
The model was trained on rainfall and streamflow data from over 500 US river basins between 1990 and 2003.
It can quantify uncertainty and absorb fresh gauge readings without retraining (inpainting).
Shen says it generally outperformed the best existing hourly deep-learning models, including on high flows, and can run in reverse to estimate rainfall from streamflow.
The paper was published in Water Resources Research; the team plans hybrid training and more physical variables.
Their earlier model worked at a daily scale, which misses hour-scale peaks such as the Central Texas floods of summer 2025.
quote_evidence: Employing the same techniques used by AI image generators, a team of researchers is building new hourly prediction methods for flash floods
We can inject new, almost real-time information into our model
Shen said their diffusion approach generally outperformed the best existing hourly deep-learning models
why_it_matters_hint: Better hourly flood forecasts could give communities more warning.
notes: University press release; performance claims are the team's. Not an operational system.
